item.title: I Said Nothing When They Came For Laurence Fox, Russell Brand And Andrew Tate, And No One Will Come For Me Because My Side Has Won The Culture
item.description:
By Liam Riestead-Schittlieb

First they came for Laurence Fox.

I said nothing because Laurence Fox had expressed several opinions in an insufficiently apologetic tone and had therefore removed himself from the protections ordinarily extended to artists.

Then they came for Russell Brand.

I said nothing because his political migration had rendered every allegation against him not only credible, but culturally useful.

Then they came for Andrew Tate.

I said nothing because Andrew Tate was Andrew Tate, and because every moral principle deserves at least one exception large enough to establish that it is not really a principle.

item.title: We Don't Have “Enough 1776” In Australia—And That's A Good Thing
item.description:
By Liam Riestead-Schittlieb (he/him) | Opinions expressed are those of the author and may become mandatory following consultation.

There are “libertarian political commentators” in Australia—whatever that means; it is probably just big words for “wankers”—who use the slogan:

Too much 1984, not enough 1776

It appears on T-shirts, podcasts and X profiles.

There is only one problem.

This is Australia.

You do not have free speech here. Natural rights are not guaranteed. Government by consent is not guaranteed.

item.title: I Don’t Post About Candidate Experience On LinkedIn Because I’m Not A Pussy
item.description:
By Ryan Hollis

There is a certain kind of LinkedIn post that appears every few weeks, usually from someone who has just completed seven rounds of interviews, performed a live coding exercise, submitted a blood sample, explained how their personal values align with “customer obsession”, and then been left staring into the void by a recruiter who has discovered the ancient corporate art of saying nothing.

The post usually begins with “Candidate experience matters”.

item.title: Building Data Centres In Other People’s Suburbs Is A Price I’m Willing To Pay
item.description:
I have thought deeply about Australia’s growing data centre debate, and after careful consideration I have reached a principled position.

Build them.

Build hundreds.

Build them wherever necessary.

Just not near me.

Some people say data centres consume too much electricity, strain the grid, require enormous water and cooling infrastructure, generate noise, increase demand for transmission upgrades, and turn otherwise liveable areas into humming concrete shrines to server load.

To those people I say: yes, probably.
